1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The EJR condition requires that no coalition \(S\) of size at least \(\ell\cdot n/k=2\ell\) can be \(\ell\)-cohesive (i.e., share at least \(\ell\) commonly approved candidates) while every member of \(S\) receives strictly fewer than \(\ell\) representatives.  

The only 3-cohesive coalition is the six voters \(\{1,2,3,8,9,10\}\) whose common approvals are exactly \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\). Consequently at least one voter in this coalition must obtain three or more seats. When exactly two of the \(x\)-candidates are chosen, voters 8-10 can obtain at most two seats; the only way to satisfy the coalition is therefore to give voter 2 (or voter 3) his or her private \(y\)-candidate, so voter 1 ends up with exactly those two \(x\)-candidates. When only one \(x\)-candidate is chosen, voter 1 himself must receive both of his private candidates \(y_1\) and \(z_3\) to reach three seats; he therefore obtains three seats. Zero \(x\)-candidates make it impossible for any member of the coalition to reach three seats, violating EJR. Hence the number of voter-1-approved members cannot fall below 2.

The four voters \(\{4,5,6,7\}\) form a 2-cohesive coalition whose common approvals are \(\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}\). A committee consisting solely of voter 1's five approved candidates contains none of those \(y\)-candidates, so every member of the coalition receives zero seats and EJR is violated. Replacing one of voter 1's candidates by two of the \(y_4,y_5,y_6\) restores EJR while still giving voter 1 four seats. Thus the attainable range for voter 1 is exactly [2,4], i.e., answer A.

(The same bounds are realized by concrete size-5 committees that also satisfy all smaller-coalition EJR constraints, confirming that no further tightening occurs.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The EJR condition requires that any voter group \(S\) of size at least \(\ell \cdot 2\) that commonly approves \(\ell\) candidates must be represented by at least \(\ell\) members of \(W\) drawn from the union of their approval sets.

The six voters approving \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\) form such a group for \(\ell=3\), so \(W\) must contain at least three candidates from their collective union \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_3\}\). The four voters approving \(\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}\) form a group for \(\ell=2\), so \(W\) must contain at least two candidates from \(\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}\).

These two constraints can be met simultaneously by sets such as
\[
W=\{y_2,y_3,z_1,y_4,y_5\}
\]
(three candidates from the first union, two from the second). This committee intersects voter 1’s ballot in the empty set, showing that the minimum is 0. Replacing two of the non-voter-1 candidates by \(y_1\) and \(z_3\) yields an EJR committee that intersects voter 1’s ballot in three candidates; substituting any fourth candidate approved by voter 1 necessarily drops the y-group representation below two, so the maximum is 3.

Thus the feasible range for voter 1 is 0–3 (choice L).

(The same range is obtained after exhaustive enumeration of all other minimal-size combinations satisfying both EJR quotas.)
